Ordinal Gates, Cardinal Bets: Matching LLM Confidence to the Financial Decision Operator

Conference: ; ;
Rayansh Singh Affiliation: Michigan State University, East Lansing, USA email: singhr26@msu.edu and Sara Rezaeimanesh Affiliation: Michigan State University, East Lansing, USA email: rezaeima@msu.edu
Abstract.

LLM confidence scores are not independently deployable objects: their decision value depends on the downstream operator and exposure controller that consume them. Monotone recalibration cannot change a coverage-matched rank-based gate, whereas position sizing consumes score magnitude, so changing a confidence map can invalidate a scale fitted to the previous score distribution. We test this on FactSet news for Nasdaq-100 equities, fitting maps and scales on 2021 and evaluating nine open-weight LLMs out-of-sample on 2022–2023. Cross-applying raw and correctness maps with independently fitted scales shows that the two components are not portable alone: scale transfer reduces certainty-equivalent return (CER) in 8/98/9 models and produces large risk-target errors. Matching each map with its fitted scale improves ensemble CER by 9.29.2 percentage points per year under frozen-scale control (p<0.001p<0.001), and the effect remains significant when the single largest-contributing model is excluded (+5.5+5.5pp/yr), so it is not driven by one case. Under an identical adaptive-volatility controller, however, the incremental effect falls to +1.6+1.6pp/yr, with a significant controller interaction. Annual walk-forward effects are smaller, although map–scale interaction remains positive in every fold. Confidence transformations should therefore be evaluated jointly with the downstream controllers that consume them.

Keywords: 
LLM confidence, selective prediction, position sizing, calibration, financial NLP

1. Introduction

One confidence score can determine both whether an AI system acts and how strongly it acts (Chow, 1970; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017): an instruction-tuned LLM asked to classify a financial news headline as predicting an up or down next-day return returns a confidence that can either gate a position (the classical reject option) or size it. We make this distinction precise through the decision operator, the map from a confidence signal to an action, and build our central claim around it: a confidence score’s decision value is operator-relative—ordinal operators consume only its ranking, while cardinal operators consume its magnitude and therefore depend on the controller paired with it.

Prior financial-LLM work has examined directional return signals and documented confidence miscalibration (Lopez-Lira and Tang, 2026; Chen et al., 2024), while calibration research largely evaluates statistical reliability or threshold-based selection as ends in themselves (Guo et al., 2017; Naeini et al., 2015). Prior work has not directly isolated which property of the score the downstream decision actually requires. Contemporaneous work makes the distinction concrete: Iacovides et al. (2025) temperature-scale a saturated sentiment score before ranking assets into fixed portfolio quantiles (Section 2). We build on the fact that monotone calibration cannot reorder predictions (Rabanser and Papernot, 2025) and extend the observation to the less-studied cardinal case of position sizing.

Ordinal operators (coverage-matched thresholding, top-kk selection, abstention, routing) consume only rank: they are invariant to strictly increasing transformations and therefore require discrimination rather than calibrated magnitude. Cardinal operators (sizing, allocation, portfolio weighting) consume magnitude, so their scores must align with the economic target the operator requires—ideally a conditional signed payoff relative to risk, rather than correctness alone (Section 3.2). A mismatched confidence map and controller can produce a material risk-budget error, in the clearest case running a raw system at up to 2.8×2.8\times its intended risk out of sample (Section 6). This is a model-governance problem: replacing the LLM, elicitation method, or calibration map can silently invalidate an exposure controller fitted to the previous score distribution.

We test this distinction on FactSet professional-newswire headlines for Nasdaq-100 constituents (2021–2023), fitting every map, threshold, and exposure scale on 2021 and evaluating forward on 2022–2023 under look-ahead-free execution. The ordinal claim is tested across five confidence-extraction channels on two open-weight LLMs (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B); the cardinal claim is tested with verbalized confidence across a nine-model grid spanning 7–32B parameters and five model families, comparing each raw-confidence system against a matched system pairing a holding-period correctness map with its own frozen-scale controller (Section 3 details the four-system design). The ordinal analysis uses next-session classification correctness, whereas the sizing analysis fits a holding-period correctness map aligned with the implemented five-session position (Section 4.1).

Empirically, ordinal recalibration repairs reliability without changing coverage-matched rankings, while the tested confidence channels have little resolution for selective prediction (Section 5). For cardinal sizing, cross-applying confidence maps and independently fitted exposure scales produces large risk distortions, whereas pairing each map with its own fitted scale improves ensemble CER by 9.29.2pp/yr under frozen-scale control—an incremental gain that largely dissolves under an identical adaptive-volatility controller, exposing the map–scale coupling that the results section quantifies (Sections 6–6.4).

We make two contributions: (1) we formalize the consequences of the ordinal–cardinal distinction for LLM confidence in financial decisions (Section 3); and (2) we show empirically that confidence maps and fitted exposure controls are coupled rather than independently portable. The latter coupling—not the headline matched-system CER gain—is the paper’s general design implication.

Our aim is to study how confidence transformations interact with the financial operator and exposure-control procedure that consume them. We do not treat correctness as a universal sizing target or claim regime invariance.

2. Related Work

Confidence calibration and selective decisions.

Calibration research measures reliability with ECE (Naeini et al., 2015) and Brier score (Brier, 1950) and repairs it with temperature scaling (Guo et al., 2017), treating reliability as an end in itself rather than a selective-classification signal. Decision-relative calibration is itself established—Zhao et al. (2021) formalize calibration against downstream decision-makers, and Wu et al. (2026) evaluate LLM confidence by downstream utility—so our claim is narrower: two financial operators consume different properties of the same signal (rank vs. magnitude), making calibration and exposure control non-portable modules. Verbalized confidence is a studied elicitation channel (Tian and others, 2023; Xiong and others, 2024; Kadavath and others, 2022), and we make its classical distinction from refinement (DeGroot and Fienberg, 1983) decision-relative. The reject option dates to Chow (Chow, 1970), and deep selective classification to Geifman and El-Yaniv (Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017). Post-hoc recalibration routinely improves threshold-based rejection (Joy et al., 2023; Guo et al., 2017). But Rabanser and Papernot (2025) show monotone calibration cannot reorder predictions, so it cannot close the selective-classification gap; our rank-invariance result in Section 3 is the formal basis.

Financial LLMs and exposure sizing.

Contemporaneous work on FinDPO (Iacovides et al., 2025) illustrates the same gap concretely: it extracts a softmax sentiment score from class-token logits, observes the same near-00/11 overconfidence saturation we document (Section 5), and applies temperature scaling to it—yet its portfolio ranks assets by that score and equal-weights a fixed top/bottom quantile, an ordinal operator that Section 3.1 shows is invariant to exactly this fix. Other recent work examines adjacent failure modes—prompting-strategy accuracy (Vamvourellis and Mehta, 2025), positional bias (Dimino et al., 2025), and sector/size/momentum bias (Lee et al., 2025)—without asking whether a score’s magnitude is safe to consume for sizing versus ranking, and we test both sides of that distinction—the rank operator and its cardinal utility counterpart (Section 3.2)—within one LLM confidence system. Mapping a forecast into a position size is classical: mean-variance choice (Markowitz, 1952), Kelly sizing (Kelly, 1956), and the “fundamental law” (Grinold and Kahn, 2000) convert a signal into exposure via its first two moments; volatility targeting (Moreira and Muir, 2017) and parameter-uncertainty (DeMiguel et al., 2009) are handled empirically by our frozen-scale controller, fit after calibration. For look-ahead bias we adopt Glasserman and Lin’s (Glasserman and Lin, 2023) named-vs-anonymized protocol under forward execution (Section 4).

3. Theory

Setup.

A classifier emits direction D⁡(X)∈{−1,+1}D(X)\in\{-1,+1\} and confidence C⁡(X)∈[12,1]C(X)\in[\tfrac{1}{2},1] separately. Define correctness Z=𝟏[D(X)=Y]Z=\mathbf{1}[D(X)=Y] and the correctness-calibration function μ⁡(u):=P⁡(Z=1∣C=u)\mu(u):=P(Z=1\mid C=u) (Murphy, 1973; DeGroot and Fienberg, 1983).

Terminology.

We fix five terms, chained by how a confidence score becomes an exposure: map gg (raw graw=idg_{\rm raw}=\mathrm{id}, correctness gcorr=μ^g_{\rm corr}=\hat{\mu}) →\to shape hh (ϕ\phi when scale-free) →\to scale κ\kappa (a parameter, not a controller) →\to controller (shape ++ scale ++ per-name caps ++ gross normalization; e.g. the frozen-scale and adaptive-volatility controllers of Section 6) →\to system (one map ++ one controller). The four-cell experiment tests whether maps and fitted scales are compatible; we use map–controller compatibility for the broader deployment claim.

3.1. Ordinal operators: a resolution bound on gate accuracy

A coverage gate retains the top-φ\varphi fraction by score. Its accuracy gain Δacc​(τ)=P⁡(Z=1∣C≥τ)−P⁡(Z=1)\Delta_{\mathrm{acc}}(\tau)=P(Z=1\mid C\geq\tau)-P(Z=1) satisfies

(1) Δacc(τ)=φ−1Cov(μ(C),𝟏[C≥τ]),\Delta_{\mathrm{acc}}(\tau)=\varphi^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(\mu(C),\mathbf{1}[C\geq\tau]),

and by Cauchy–Schwarz, writing RES⁡(C)=Var⁡(μ⁡(C))\mathrm{RES}(C)=\operatorname{Var}(\mu(C)) for Brier resolution (Murphy, 1973),

(2) |Δacc​(τ)|≤RES⁡(C)​1−φφ.|\Delta_{\mathrm{acc}}(\tau)|\leq\sqrt{\mathrm{RES}(C)\,\tfrac{1-\varphi}{\varphi}}.

For every strictly increasing ψ\psi, the threshold family {C≥τ}τ\{C\geq\tau\}_{\tau} bijects onto {ψ(C)≥t}t\{\psi(C)\geq t\}_{t}, so the accuracy–coverage frontier, every coverage-matched portfolio, and RES\mathrm{RES} are invariant to ψ\psi. A fixed numerical threshold (confidence above 0.700.70, say) is magnitude-sensitive, not rank-only, so it falls outside this invariance result—only coverage-matched thresholds, which adapt to the score distribution, are covered. Temperature and Platt scaling are strictly increasing, so they can improve reliability but cannot change score order, RES\mathrm{RES}, or a coverage-matched gate (slopes verified positive for all 18 configurations; Section 5). Isotonic regression is only nondecreasing: it may introduce plateaus, so this exact bijection claim applies to strictly increasing ψ\psi; in our empirical isotonic check, ties within a plateau are broken deterministically by the pre-calibration raw score, which we verify preserves the coverage-matched selected set exactly (0 discrepancies across all 18 ordinal configurations and 20 coverage levels from 5% to 100%).

3.2. Cardinal operators: map-specific scales and magnitude sensitivity

The following oracle benchmark isolates why a magnitude-consuming operator can benefit from a better-aligned score even when rank is unchanged; it is not the system implemented in Section 6, and the gap between them is made explicit below. Maximizing one-period conditional quadratic utility E⁡[h⁡(C)​Q]−λ2​E​[v⁡(C)​h​(C)2]E[h(C)Q]-\tfrac{\lambda}{2}E[v(C)h(C)^{2}] (λ>0\lambda>0) over hh gives the oracle sizing rule

The cardinal target is therefore conditional signed payoff relative to risk, not correctness probability alone.

Equation (3) identifies conditional signed payoff relative to risk as the oracle target. Our primary system instead uses correctness probability as a lower-variance proxy and restricts sizing to a map-specific shape multiplied by a scalar scale. We therefore test whether changing the confidence map requires refitting that scale. Section 6.3 separately evaluates direct signed-payoff estimation.

The implemented system does not fit hh freely: it fixes a map-specific shape ϕ⁡(C)∈[0,1]\phi(C)\in[0,1] and a single scalar κ≥0\kappa\geq 0, h⁡(C)=κ​ϕ​(C)h(C)=\kappa\,\phi(C) (Section 4.3, eq. (5)). Restricting the objective above to this family, writing Yϕ:=ϕ⁡(C)​QY_{\phi}:=\phi(C)Q and vϕ:=E⁡[v⁡(C)​ϕ​(C)2]v_{\phi}:=E[v(C)\phi(C)^{2}], gives Uϕ​(κ)=κ​E​[Yϕ]−λ2​κ2​vϕU_{\phi}(\kappa)=\kappa E[Y_{\phi}]-\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\kappa^{2}v_{\phi}; when E⁡[Yϕ]>0E[Y_{\phi}]>0 the restricted optimum is κϕ⋆=E⁡[Yϕ]/(λ​vϕ)\kappa_{\phi}^{\star}=E[Y_{\phi}]/(\lambda v_{\phi}).

The empirical volatility-targeting rule κϕvol=σtarget/SD⁡(Yϕ)\kappa_{\phi}^{\mathrm{vol}}=\sigma_{\mathrm{target}}/\operatorname{SD}(Y_{\phi}) is the analogous map-specific construction (Section 6).

Scale equivariance.

Uniform positive rescaling cannot explain the matched effect because refitting the volatility scale exactly offsets it before caps bind; improvement therefore requires nonlinear reshaping, support changes, cap interactions, or different out-of-sample behavior. Thus any matched-system improvement must arise from changes in relative magnitudes or in the active-position support, rather than from a trivial global rescaling of confidence.

The four-system design.

We distinguish the confidence transformation gm​(C)g_{m}(C) from the sizing function it feeds: graw​(C)=Cg_{\rm raw}(C)=C, gcorr​(C)=μ^​(C)g_{\rm corr}(C)=\hat{\mu}(C), and hm​(C)=max⁡(0,2​gm​(C)−1)h_{m}(C)=\max(0,2g_{m}(C)-1) for either map (eq. (5)). Crossing the two confidence maps (grawg_{\rm raw}, gcorrg_{\rm corr}) with two independently fitted scales κ\kappa (raw; correctness-map) yields four systems: raw (raw map, raw scale), map-only (correctness map, raw scale), scale-transfer (raw map, correctness-map scale), and matched (correctness map, correctness-map scale). The two diagonal systems are valid map–scale pairings; the two off-diagonal systems diagnose whether a map and a scale are portable across signal distributions. The map-only cell, which holds the exposure scale fixed while the map changes, is our primary shared-scale surrogate (Figure 1).

Writing J⁡(g,κ)J(g,\kappa) for realized test-period CER under the actual caps, costs, and normalization of Section 4.3, and Jr​r,Jc​r,Jr​c,Jc​cJ_{rr},J_{cr},J_{rc},J_{cc} for the four systems, the matched effect decomposes exactly—with no distributional assumption—into map, scale, and map×\timesscale-interaction terms:

(4) Jc​c−Jr​r=(Jc​r−Jr​r)+(Jr​c−Jr​r)+(Jc​c−Jc​r−Jr​c+Jr​r).J_{cc}-J_{rr}=(J_{cr}-J_{rr})+(J_{rc}-J_{rr})+(J_{cc}-J_{cr}-J_{rc}+J_{rr}).

Section 6 estimates each component—map replacement, scale transfer, and their interaction—directly under the implemented caps, costs, and temporal split.

4. Data and Evaluation Protocol

4.1. Data, splits, and labels

We use FactSet professional-newswire headlines for Nasdaq-100 constituents (2021–2023). The cleaning pipeline restricts to US-equity, English-language wire items, strips source prefixes, and drops routine ownership/sector calendar notices. The unit of analysis is the (ticker, trading-day). All headlines for a ticker-day are aggregated into one bundle (mean 4.174.17/bundle, median 22). Calibration is 2021 (15,03415{,}034 ticker-days) and evaluation is 2022–2023 (31,88831{,}888 ticker-days, 505505 test-period trading sessions). Every recalibration parameter, temperature, frozen-scale controller, and gate threshold θ⋆\theta^{\star} is fit only on 2021. We run named and anonymized conditions (company names/tickers masked with [COMPANY] before the LLM sees the text) as separate configurations throughout.

FactSet does not provide granular intraday timestamps, so a ticker-day bundle dated DD is assigned to the first trading session strictly after DD–session TT–to eliminate same-session execution. The ordinal experiment (Section 5) evaluates whether the predicted direction matches that session’s own open-to-close return sign. The cardinal experiment (Section 6) sizes a five-session position, so its downstream-success map instead estimates whether that same predicted direction matches the five-session holding-period return sign. This is a decision-aligned success target, not a recalibration of the original one-session prediction. The exact ordinal invariance result is horizon-independent; the one-session gate is the classification-aligned illustration, whereas the five-session target corresponds to the implemented holding-period decision (direct payoff estimation targets this quantity directly; Section 6.3 compares it to correctness calibration). Five sessions was fixed a priori as the primary weekly holding cadence. A descriptive twelve-horizon sensitivity sweep places h=5h{=}5 within a broad stable region: out-of-sample matched effects remain positive through h=8h{=}8 and attenuate at longer horizons; no multiplicity-adjusted inference is claimed across horizons.

Primary sample and temporal extension.

The primary nine-model evaluation (Section 6) uses the 2021–2023 sample above. The temporal extension (Section 6.4) evaluates a five-model subset11 1 Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B, Phi-4, Mistral-24B, and Gemma3-27B. spanning model families and parameter scales on 12,91112{,}911 additional FactSet 2024–2025 ticker-days using four annual walk-forward folds. Each fold fits the confidence map and both exposure scales on year tt and evaluates them frozen on year t+1t{+}1, holding horizon, costs, caps, universe, and γ\gamma fixed. Signals whose five-session hold crosses the calibration-year boundary are dropped, not truncated, and bootstrap blocks are sampled within fold boundaries. Each test year is forward-held-out relative to its calibration fit, though not necessarily relative to model pretraining.

4.2. Models and confidence signals

Ordinal grid.

Qwen2.5-7B and Gemma-2-9B across five confidence-extraction channels, chosen because they preserve different statistical properties of the same model: some rank well but are miscalibrated, others the reverse, making the operator-relative claim testable rather than definitionally true of one extraction method. Verbalized (regex-parsed “Direction/Confidence,” parse-failure 2.62.6–3.5%3.5\%, recorded as missing and excluded from that ticker-day’s active signal set, never imputed), two-token logit (Δ​z=log⁡pup−log⁡pdown\Delta z=\log p_{\textsc{up}}-\log p_{\textsc{down}}, predicted-class confidence σ⁡(|Δ​z|)\sigma(|\Delta z|)), logit-full (full-vocabulary up/down probability mass), logit-ent (normalized negentropy of the first-token distribution), and P(True) (Qwen2.5 only (Kadavath and others, 2022)); a K=5K{=}5 temperature-sampled self-consistency baseline (Wang and others, 2022) is reported separately as an additional baseline, outside this family. The four channels common to both models give 16 configurations, and Qwen-only P(True) in both conditions adds two, for 18 model×\timescondition configurations across the five primary channels—the accuracy-tuned family tested jointly in Section 5.

Cardinal grid.

Nine unmodified HuggingFace open-weight checkpoints22 2 Models: Qwen2.5-{7B,14B,32B}, Gemma-2-9B, Gemma-3-27B, Mistral-{7B,24B}, Phi-4, and FinLLaMa-8B. spanning 7–32B parameters across five model families (Qwen, Gemma, Mistral, Phi-4, FinLLaMa), using verbalized confidence, the only channel consistently available across all checkpoints. The 2025 extension corpus (Section 6.4) postdates the two primary models’ release, ruling out pretraining-data inclusion for them. Pretraining-cutoff audit status for the other seven is a limitation (Section 7).

Implementation.

Each bundle is rendered as a single user-role chat-template turn (no system prompt), truncated to 512 input tokens. Multi-headline bundles are pipe-joined. Verbalized decoding is greedy. The logit channel is a single forward pass with no generation. Models ≥24\geq 24B parameters run int8-quantized; all others run unquantized float16. All random seeds are fixed to 42. The verbalized channel asks the model to predict UP or DOWN and report an integer confidence from 0 to 100 (50 = completely uncertain).

Realized portfolio constraints were never binding: mean daily gross exposure was 85.2%85.2\%, with a 95%95\%th percentile of 98.1%98.1\% and maximum of 99.8%99.8\%; per-name caps were never exceeded.

Evidentiary status.

The pre-specified primary economic estimand is the 2021-fit/2022–2023 matched-versus-raw ensemble effect under frozen-scale control; alternative calibrators, model exclusions, placebos, controller choice, costs, and annual transfer are confirmatory robustness checks, while the fixed-2024H1, diagnostic-correlation, label-noise, and subgroup analyses are exploratory.

5. Ordinal Decisions

Calibration without decision change.

Taking softmax⁡([zup,zdown])\mathrm{softmax}([z_{\textsc{up}},\allowbreak z_{\textsc{down}}]) on two vocabulary logits and using the max as confidence saturates: LLM vocabulary logits routinely differ by 20+20+ nats, collapsing confidence to ≈0.97\approx 0.97–0.980.98 and ECE to ≈0.47\approx 0.47 (both models, both conditions). Fitting one temperature TT per model on the calib split repairs this: logit ECE falls to 0.030.03–0.040.04. Because softmax and σ⁡(Δ​z/T)\sigma(\Delta z/T) are both strictly increasing in Δ​z\Delta z, they induce the identical ranking (Section 3.1): the coverage-matched gate is exactly unchanged even though ECE moves by an order of magnitude.

Low resolution limits selective gains.

Resolution—the degree to which confidence separates observations with different conditional success rates—is the quantity a coverage gate needs. The Murphy decomposition makes the binding constraint precise: with UNC=p¯​(1−p¯)≈0.249\mathrm{UNC}=\bar{p}(1-\bar{p})\approx 0.249, resolution is small everywhere, RES/UNC\mathrm{RES}/\mathrm{UNC} ranging 0.07%0.07\%–0.4%0.4\% across all 18 configurations, and the base classifier itself is weak (1-session accuracy 50.350.3–51.8%51.8\%, at or below the 53.8%53.8\% base rate). Bound (2) caps the accuracy gain any coverage gate can extract from resolution this low: at the 10%10\% coverage floor used below, roughly 44–99 percentage points even at best-resolution. The same conclusion holds across the five primary channels (verbalized, three logit variants, and P(True)); none provides enough resolution for dependable selection. A K=5K{=}5 temperature-sampled self-consistency baseline (Wang and others, 2022), reported separately, adds none—its outputs are unanimous on 9696–98%98\% of ticker-days.

Fixed-threshold gating yields no reliable economic lift.

Fixed numerical thresholds fall outside the rank-invariance result above because they consume score magnitude. Thresholds fitted on 2021 either for accuracy or CER nevertheless yield no family-wise significant 2022–2023 improvement: 0/18 accuracy-tuned configurations survive Romano–Wolf correction, and 0/18 CER-tuned configurations survive Holm correction despite 15/18 positive point estimates. Thus, recalibration cannot change coverage-matched selection, while the available score rankings are too weak to support reliable fixed-threshold gains.

6. Cardinal Decisions

6.1. Maps and scales are not independently portable

Portability diagnosis.

Maps and exposure scales perform poorly when transferred independently.

Cross-applying each map with each fitted scale (Figure 1, right) shows neither is portable alone: map replacement at the raw scale is Holm-significant in only 2/92/9 models, while the correctness-map scale applied to the raw map reduces CER in 8/98/9. The resulting model-ensemble map–scale interaction (eq. (4)’s last term) is +17.1+17.1pp/yr; we interpret this interaction descriptively rather than causally. Consistent with map-specific scaling, the correctness-map scale realizes 11.8%11.8\% mean per-model test volatility when transferred to the raw map, versus 8.4%8.4\% with its intended correctness map. Conversely, the raw-map scale realizes 9.8%9.8\% with its intended raw map but only 3.3%3.3\% when transferred to the correctness map. Holding the scale fixed while changing the confidence map therefore shifts realized risk sharply in either direction; matching reduces transfer distortion but does not eliminate fit-to-test risk drift. The next two subsections show what pairing each map with its own fitted scale buys back, and how much of that recovery is magnitude reallocation versus filtering. Applying the correctness map to a coverage-matched gate, meanwhile, leaves the portfolio unchanged, as predicted by Section 3.1.

6.2. Matched map–scale pairing improves the frozen system

Matched pairing reduces transfer distortion.

Pairing each holding-period correctness map with its own fitted frozen-scale controller removes the cross-map scale mismatch diagnosed in Section 6.1 and improves ensemble CER by 9.29.2pp/yr.

We compare each raw system (raw map, own fitted κ\kappa) with the corresponding matched system (correctness map, own fitted κ\kappa), condition-averaging named and anonymized inputs; the off-diagonal systems of Section 6.1 serve as portability diagnostics. The map-specific scalar benchmark of Section 3.2 predicts that scales are generally not portable across maps, but whether the correctness diagonal outperforms the raw diagonal under estimated scales, caps, costs, and temporal shift is an empirical question we estimate directly across the nine models (Section 4.2).

Of the model-ensemble +9.2+9.2pp/yr effect, +9.0+9.0 is attributable to the mean-return component and +0.2+0.2 to the variance component. The matched improvement is positive in 9/99/9 models, and 3/93/9 (Qwen2.5-7B, Mistral-24B, Gemma3-27B) individually survive Holm correction. The joint effect is strongly significant (p<0.001p<0.001). Realized volatility falls in 9/99/9. The model-ensemble effect also remains positive and significant excluding Qwen2.5-7B (+5.5+5.5pp/yr, 95% CI [1.0,10.1][1.0,10.1], p=0.015p=0.015, same joint-bootstrap method); Qwen2.5-7B’s large contribution does not alone drive the model-ensemble result. The model-ensemble raw system returns 3.9%3.9\%/yr versus 12.9%12.9\%/yr for the matched system (Table 2). Beta regression in place of isotonic gives an almost identical effect (+9.4+9.4pp/yr, CI [4.9,14.3][4.9,14.3]), with more models Holm-significant (5/95/9 vs. 3/93/9).

Case study: Qwen2.5-7B

Qwen exhibits the clearest mismatch: its raw system realizes 11.711.7–13.8%13.8\% volatility against the shared 5%5\% calibration target, running at 2.32.3–2.8×2.8\times its intended risk. Its full contribution is included in the +9.2+9.2pp/yr headline effect; we treat the case as an illustrative governance failure of the raw system rather than as a caveat on the matched system’s validity. Excluding it entirely, the ensemble effect remains +5.5+5.5pp/yr [1.0,10.1][1.0,10.1], so the result is not driven by one case.

Raw confidence adds little beyond sign-only sizing: −0.8-0.8pp/yr CER for sign-only versus +2.7+2.7pp/yr for the LLM’s own uncalibrated magnitude (Table 2). The gain appears once the correctness map is paired with its own frozen-scale controller (κ\kappa fitted during calibration and frozen during evaluation; +12.0+12.0pp/yr), also reducing maximum drawdown from −11.7%-11.7\% to −4.9%-4.9\% and improving daily 5%5\% expected shortfall from −1.26%-1.26\% to −1.03%-1.03\%.

We also test an adaptive-volatility controller that re-scales κ\kappa online in non-overlapping 2121-session (∼\simmonthly) blocks toward the same 5%5\% target: after each block it applies a multiplicative log-scale update log⁡κb+1=log⁡κb−γ​eb\log\kappa_{b+1}=\log\kappa_{b}-\gamma\,e_{b}, where ebe_{b} is the prior block’s realized-versus-target annualized-volatility gap, using only pre-block information and clipping κ\kappa to [0.2,5]×[0.2,5]\times the frozen scale (learning rate γ\gamma fit on 2021). Under this controller the correctness map still exceeds raw (+8.2+8.2 vs. +6.6+6.6pp/yr). The matched map thus adds substantial value under the frozen-scale controller, but only limited and statistically imprecise incremental value under the adaptive-volatility controller (Section 6.3).

6.3. Magnitude reallocation, not filtering, drives most of the matched effect

Mechanism check.

Most of the matched effect remains when the raw and correctness-map systems are forced onto common trade support.

Because h⁡(u)=max⁡(0,2​u−1)h(u)=\max(0,2u-1) embeds a boundary at u=0.5u=0.5, the full rule may benefit from removing trades as well as reallocating magnitude. We therefore isolate three systems, each with its own fitted κ\kappa: gate-only (h(u)=𝟏[μ^(u)>0.5]h(u)=\mathbf{1}[\hat{\mu}(u)>0.5], equal weight among retained positions, all magnitude information discarded), common-support (h⁡(u)=max⁡(0,2​μ^​(u)−1)h(u)=\max(0,2\hat{\mu}(u)-1) with zeros replaced by the smallest positive calibration-split size, preserving every raw active position), and the full matched system.

The matched effect remains positive across alternative raw sizing maps and seven model-family compositions, while direct-payoff estimation exceeds correctness calibration in 1010 of 1818 conditions.

Robustness.

Table 3 tests three alternative explanations. Forcing common trade support leaves most of the gain intact, so magnitude reallocation rather than filtering drives the result; dispersion matching alone recovers little of isotonic’s gain; and although joint map–scale refitting has a positive shuffled-label baseline, the observed effect exceeds both unrestricted and within-date shuffled-label refits. Temporal-shift and wrong-ticker placebos likewise eliminate the effect, and net exposure and market beta change little across books. A Newey–West regression of the matched-minus-raw spread on tech (non-tech minus tech), momentum, and volatility terciles leaves an annualized intercept of +8.6+8.6pp/yr [3.2,14.1][3.2,14.1], unexplained by these exposures.

Deployment boundary (adaptive controller).

Against a label-free adaptive-volatility-only baseline (the raw map under the adaptive controller defined above), the matched system is directionally better in 9/99/9 models; the estimate is positive but statistically imprecise (Table 3). A paired test of per-model effects across the two controllers confirms that the matched-system effect is significantly larger under frozen-scale control (interaction: +7.78+7.78pp/yr, 95% CI [2.01,15.25][2.01,15.25], p<0.001p<0.001).

6.4. Temporal transfer depends on fitting regime

Deployment boundary (annual transfer).

Annual refitting yields smaller net gains because positive map–scale interaction is offset by adverse scale transfer.

We evaluate temporal transfer under two protocols. Under the annual walk-forward protocol of Section 4 (refit on year tt, evaluate frozen on t+1t{+}1; five models, named and anonymized), all three calibrators are directionally positive but none survives family-wise Holm correction (p=0.144p=0.144, 0.0580.058, 0.1230.123 for isotonic, Beta, Platt; Beta most precise; Table 4). Transfer is therefore positive but attenuated and estimator-dependent rather than regime-invariant. The exploratory fixed-window protocol instead refits once on 2024H1 and produces larger isotonic effects in 2024H2 and 2025 (+21.3+21.3 and +15.7+15.7pp/yr; nominal, uncorrected), reinforcing sensitivity to calibration-window choice. The attenuation coincides with a deterioration in the confidence signal: pooled Murphy resolution (RES/UNC) for the five-model verbalized channel falls from 0.170.17–0.19%0.19\% in 2022–2023 to 0.040.04–0.08%0.08\% in 2024–2025, consistent with contemporaneous evidence of weakening LLM return predictability (Lopez-Lira and Tang, 2026). Correctness–payoff alignment likewise falls sharply (Figure 2, top: 1.001.00/0.830.83/0.940.94 in 2022–2024, 0.260.26 in 2025). These diagnostics do not explain the fold-level Δ\DeltaCER pattern, however: the weakest fold (20232023, −0.70-0.70pp/yr) has the best resolution and second-best alignment, coinciding instead with an unusually strong underlying-universe return (+28.7%+28.7\% annualized) under net-long books. We therefore treat resolution and alignment as descriptive rather than causal explanations of transfer.

Decomposing the walk-forward effect.

Under isotonic calibration, the pooled annual effect decomposes into −4.0-4.0pp/yr from map replacement, −8.1-8.1pp/yr from scale transfer, and +13.3+13.3pp/yr from their interaction (eq. (4), fold-respecting block bootstrap): the small net gain reflects offsetting components rather than the disappearance of map–scale dependence, and the interaction is positive in every fold.

7. Limitations and Conclusion

Signal quality.

The base classifier is weak (50.350.3–51.8%51.8\% accuracy vs. a 53.8%53.8\% base rate), so we make no market-beating claim and treat Table 2’s sign-only book as the relevant floor comparator. Correctness is used only as the lower-variance payoff proxy described in Section 3.2; pooled diagnostics across all 1818 configurations (Figure 2, bottom) show fitted correctness and signed payoff generally rising together, but do not establish this relationship within every model or masking condition. Because joint refitting has a positive shuffled-label baseline (Section 6.3), the +9.2+9.2pp/yr effect is best read as evidence for the fitted system rather than a purely information-driven effect.

Temporal validity.

All nine models were released after the primary 20222022–20232023 evaluation period, so pretraining exposure to those market outcomes cannot be completely ruled out; only the 2025 observations are verified to postdate the release dates of the two primary models (Qwen2.5-7B, Gemma-2-9B), and training-cutoff audit status for the other seven is not fully documented. A named-vs-anonymized comparison shows no gap (+9.1+9.1 vs. +9.4+9.4pp/yr, pooled): if the gain were ticker-identity memorization, masking names/tickers should attenuate it; it does not. More fundamentally, the paper’s central claim does not require the 20222022–20232023 trading gain to be contamination-free: the map–scale coupling result (Section 6.1) follows from how a fixed rule responds to a confidence-map change (Section 3), not any one period’s return sign or size. Contamination could inflate the headline effect’s magnitude but not the analytical non-portability result. We cannot rule out contamination that does not require entity recognition (e.g., recalled macro/sector narratives), and annual walk-forward gains are smaller and do not survive family-wise correction (Section 6.4).

Generalizability.

Only 33 of 99 per-model effects individually survive Holm, so the result concerns matched-system levels and map–scale compatibility, not per-model significance. Pre-declared partitions concentrate essentially all of the primary-period gain in 20222022 (+16.2+16.2pp/yr, p<0.001p<0.001) and non-technology tickers (+13.9+13.9pp/yr, p=0.002p=0.002, 34/6134/61 names), with 20232023 and technology names both insignificant—a real but partial tilt, not a full explanation of the effect (factor regression, Section 6.3). The five-session hold was fixed a priori as the primary weekly cadence; the twelve-horizon sensitivity sweep (Section 4.1) is descriptive and not covered by the Holm/Romano–Wolf corrections, and results are stable under 11–3%3\% annual short-borrow costs (model-ensemble gains +9.5+9.5–9.89.8pp/yr).

Conclusion.

Monotone recalibration does not affect coverage-matched gates because it preserves score ordering. Position sizing is different: changing the confidence map changes portfolio exposures and may invalidate a scale fitted to the original score distribution. In our data, matching the map and scale materially improves the frozen-scale system; the benefit attenuates under adaptive risk control and later walk-forward evaluation. Confidence maps should therefore be monitored and revalidated as part of the full portfolio-construction system.
